what_it_does: Radio transmitters that broadcast digital signals face a tradeoff: they either spend a lot of power on conversion hardware or they introduce nonlinearity (signals that distort). This paper describes a 'digital polar transmitter'—a power-efficient radio chip that converts digital symbols directly into amplitude and phase signals for 256-QAM modulation (a dense way to encode data), using only 1-bit pulse-density modulation (a way to encode signals using single-bit on-off switching). The key innovation is eliminating the CORDIC converter (a traditional but power-hungry circuit for coordinate conversion) and instead using phase modulation based on edge selection, which is simpler and inherently linear. The power amplifier itself runs at 1-bit resolution, avoiding the efficiency losses of switched-capacitor designs that are common in existing low-power transmitters.
